utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Before we invite the Defence to call its next witness, Mr. Stewart, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- exhibits tendered by the Prosecution in relation to witness Mrs. Cenic, are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then P1139 up to and including P1144 are admitted into evidence. The Chamber, meanwhile, has received the response of the Prosecution on protective measures for the next witness to come, not for this one. The Chamber -- it was not obvious to us that any additional information by the Defence had been included, or perhaps it was not given.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There was a change from the factual position when we were discussing this in Court, because at that time, if Your Honours recall, the witness was expected very imminently to arrive, but the timetable's been changed, so since that witness isn't -- isn't here yet --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- we've been dealing with it in a different way. We will supply the Trial Chamber with such additional information as we have in answer to the points raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then as far as I know, there are no other procedural issues to be dealt with at this moment, so therefore, Madam Usher, could you please escort the next witness into the courtroom. I'm expecting, Mr. Stewart, that you're ready to call this next witness, which I do understand is Mr. Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. It's Mr. Nenad Kecmanovic. [Interpretation] This witness is going to be speaking French. He's not going to be speaking French, no. He understands French, but he doesn't understand any English. So as you say in Paris, "c'est comme ca."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, be very careful, because maybe Judge Hanoteau is going to speak even more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's get serious again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We're just waiting for the witness, Your Honour, I assume, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kecmanovic, I take it. Could I invite you just to remain standing for a second. I'd like to invite you, in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher now hands out the text of this solemn declaration to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kecmanovic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined by Mr. Stewart -- Mr. Stewart, I take it. Yes. By Mr. Stewart, who is counsel for the Defence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, I'm going to put a number of I hope relatively straightforward factual points to you to seek your agreement. You -- you were born in Sarajevo in 1947, and you are now a professor of politics at Belgrade University, a post that you've held for about five years?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you've lived your whole life in Sarajevo until July 1992, and up to that time -- not your whole life, but at that time you were a professor of politics at Sarajevo University; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And your -- you and your family currently live in Belgrade, although you are officially resident in Sarajevo, although you've not been back there since 1992?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have two residences and two nationalities, and I still own an apartment in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, going back to before the war, you were active in politics as a member of the Communist Party up to 1989; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in 1986, you'd been a candidate to be the Bosnia-Herzegovina member of the joint Presidency of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But your candidacy was undermined by a secret service report that you were a British spy?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: More or less that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was it true that you were a British spy?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You joined Ante Markovic's Alliance of Reform Forces - it goes under a number of different names, but commonly known as the SRS - on its formation in the summer of 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you, around that time, made any offer in relation to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was invited by the group that founded the SDS to come and be its leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the members of that group who issued the invitation were who?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Those were mostly people who constituted the top leadership of the SDS and Serbian national movement, like Mr. Koljevic, Radovan Karadzic, Vojislav Maksimovic, Aleksa Buha, Professor Ekmecic, who was one of the founders but formally he never had any position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik come into that picture at all at that time?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik was not a member of the inner circle of those who founded the Serbian Democratic Party. I didn't know him from before. He was not a public figure, and he was not a member of that group that had established the Serbian Democratic Party, as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you ever -- have you ever joined the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: My response was that I supported the foundation of that party because the other two peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina had already established their ethnically-based parties, and in that sense I supported the foundation of the SDS, but I said that I wouldn't be ready to lead that party and that I would probably not even become its member because I -- I had become the president of Markovic's party, the Party of Reformists. I was its president for Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was a Yugoslav party; Markovic was its leader at the level of Yugoslavia, and I was its leader in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that moment, this was all in the pipeline. There were talks about that, but later on this was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Without embarking on any detailed analysis, is it -- is it possible for you to summarise what you saw as the essential differences between the SDS and the party, the SRS, that you joined at that time?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Alliance of Reformists, as it was called, was a party which was one of the rare parties -- or the only big party that still fought to preserve Yugoslavia. The League of Communists, as it was known at the time, had already broken apart and segmented into republican parties, and Markovic's party insisted on the preservation of Yugoslavia. That was one element that went into the picture. And the second element was that it was not an ethnically-based party. It was a multi-ethnic party, unlike the SDS, the HDZ, the SDA. Those were ethnically-based parties. The SDS was the same. And the third element which constituted a difference was the fact that all the parties at that moment advocated democratisation, liberalisation, the market economy, and so on and so forth. However, it was believed that the reformists had more advantage in that respect because Ante Markovic had been Prime Minister, and he had proven himself as a person who knew how to implement that plan. He had been successful as a Prime Minister at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then, coming to the November 1990 multi-party elections, your party won about -- about ten or so seats in the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly at those elections. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Eleven, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But you didn't stand for election as a deputy in the Assembly, but you stood for election to the Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you just missed out on being elected; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the third ranking by the number of votes, following Mrs. Plavsic and the late Nikola Koljevic. The difference was very small, but big enough for not -- for me not to become a member of the Presidency because only two members were elected into the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the position was this, wasn't it: That Mr. Abdic, Mr. Izetbegovic, and Mr. Ganic were elected?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You recall that Mr. Abdic, Mr. Izetbegovic, and Mr. Ganic were among those elected to the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked you what your question was because I wanted to avoid any confusion. The three members of the Muslim people were elected as opposed to two Croats and two Serbs. Mr. Ganic was actually elected as a representative of other parties; not as a Muslim, not as a Bosniak but as the representative of the other peoples who were present in Bosnia and Herzegovina but did not form any of the constituent people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He declared himself as a Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you've anticipated my next question, so I'll just complete the whole list then. Mr. Abdic, Mr. Izetbegovic declared themselves as Muslims. They were members of the SDA, and they were elected; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Ganic was a member of the SDA, but, as you say, declared himself as a Yugoslav and was elected?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: At first Mr. Ganic was a member of the same party that I led, and then on the eve of the elections he became a member of the SDA, and the SDA put him up as a Yugoslav candidate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic, as you've indicated, were both members of the SDS, both Serbs, of course, and were both elected. And members of the HDZ, Mr. Kljuic -- Stjepan Kljuic and Mr. Franjo Boras, two Croats, were also elected to the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And as far as Serbs were concerned, you were the next in votes after the successful candidates Koljevic and Plavsic, ahead of the next unsuccessful Serb candidate, Mr. Pejanovic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- after the multi-party elections it was conventional, was it, and you followed that convention, for you as a senior member of your party to attend Assembly sessions, even though, of course not being a deputy, you didn't have a vote?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And another person who attended and the two of you were able, apart from not having the voting status, were able to participate actively included you and Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Before Mr. Krajisnik -- or when Mr. Krajisnik became president of the Assembly, we've already heard some evidence that Mr. Trbojevic had been a possibility but had not taken that post. Can you recall any other names of people who were potential presidents of the Assembly under discussion at that time?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can give you a few names. One of them was my colleague from the school of philosophy, Professor Aleksa Buha; then from the school of literature, Professor Vojislav Maksimovic; a lawyer, Trbojevic, who you've already mentioned; and a few other people were in the game but I can't remember their names at the moment. Those were representatives of the SDS to whom that position was offered before it was offered to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had you, before he became the president of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly, had you met Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you make any inquiries about Mr. Krajisnik when he took over that position?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik was one of the rare people who were highly positioned in the new government whom I had not known personally before. And I heard that he was one of the managers in Energoinvest, which was a large Sarajevo-based company. I inquired about him. I asked some people who knew him about him, and I received some basic information about him before I actually met him in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what -- what information did you receive about him?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The opinions were positive. My Croatian and Muslim friends told me that he was professionally very successful, that he was a very good manager. He was the financial manager of one of the companies within the Energoinvest company. And given the position in the national party, I was interested in that aspect because I also heard that he was a very patriotic person, that he was very religious, that he expresses his national views very freely, but also that he expected the religious and national identity of his colleagues and people that worked with him. I also remember a very interesting detail: At that time, it was not customary for people to congratulate each other's religious holidays, but he did that, and he offered everybody to take a day off on the biggest religious holidays to celebrate them. My friends to whom I spoke, although they did not feel the need to take any days off, still thought this was a very noble gesture on Krajisnik's part. And as I say, at the time it was not customary to take or to get a day off on religious holidays.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, the Assembly, the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly as constituted after the November 1990 elections, was the -- it was the first multi-party Assembly in, well, in effective living memory, wasn't it, in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm afraid I haven't understood your question properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- after the November 1990 elections, the -- the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina was, for all practical purposes, the first multi-party Assembly in living memory, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did this -- did this have public impact in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it did for my generation and for people somewhat older and younger than me, the post-war generation. That is this was a very interesting experience. This was more than a political event, it was a political spectacle, because the sessions of the parliament, of the multi-party parliament, were broadcast on television, whereas the other bodies, which also are multi-party bodies, such as the government, did not receive that much attention of the TV. There were just short reports from the meetings of those bodies. The Assembly sessions were broadcast in total, live. The Assembly, in communist tradition, was a boring body. Its session were boring because it was a mono-party, and all of a sudden the citizens were able to directly follow political debates which involved a national or inter -- intra-national component.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the -- overall, the public reaction to the new Assembly was, from what you've just described, distinctly positive, was it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the first multi-party elections, which took a while, this was a direct continuous experience of democracy or how democracy should look like in everyday life, and this was presented to the eyes of regular citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How far did Mr. Krajisnik make a contribution to that public view of the new Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think -- and not just me; this was a prevalent opinion at the time among the citizens irrespective of their ethnic affiliation or political background -- that his contribution was a major one, because he was not an authoritarian president of the Assembly. He channeled the work of the Assembly very correctly. Whenever he interrupted, it was in accordance with the book of rules. But he would rarely do that. He was very relaxed in his role, and the assemblymen were given an opportunity to speak at great length. Sometimes those sessions were funny because the deputies on all the three sides were new to the politics, and the way the politics were run were also -- was also new. All this was a novelty for an average person, and I believe that Mr. Krajisnik was the one who instigated that spirit, who encouraged that spirit. He did not want to restrict the debates. On the other hand, the sessions lasted very long, but he would allow for longer breaks and then the atmosphere of the meeting room would spill over to the Assembly building corridors where there would be journalists with cameras, and all this was part of a very lively event.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's -- it's true, isn't it, Mr. Kecmanovic, that Assembly sessions under Mr. Krajisnik's chairmanship tended often to last a very long time?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: They lasted a long time. I'm talking about the period from the elections until the beginning of the war, which was very short. There was a comment that could be heard among the people, especially when the war was already in the air. People would tend to say for as long as Krajisnik chairs the Assembly meetings, there is no danger of war, because everybody was always there. There was just one permanent Assembly session. There is either a session or a long break. This was the comment, the prevalent comment to those long sessions, which were either in progress or on a break. Actually, those sessions would take over a few days normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the time of the 19 -- November 1990 election when Mr. Krajisnik then became the president of the Assembly, at that point what was the relative public standing of Professor Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic, and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Again I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'll put it a different way. Professor Koljevic, was he a known political figure already by November 1990?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: When you ask me about my candidacy, I have to say that it was customary for people to be appointed to the positions in the state Presidency if they had already occupied leading positions in their respective parties, and in that sense Professor Koljevic and Mrs. Biljana Plavsic were party favourites. They were highly positioned in their party. That's why they became candidates for the Presidency. And they took up that position as a result of the fact that they were members of the inner circle of those who had established the party from day one and that outside of the political context they were public figures and they were well known in the life of Sarajevo, Sarajevo which was the capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mrs. Plavsic was the dean of the School of the Natural Sciences and Mathematics. She was also a highly positioned official of the Socialist Alliance of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was an organisation that rallied all those who were not affiliated with any party at a high political level. She was in charge of the sector of education and science. In other words, she was a publicly known figure. Professor Koljevic, given his profession and his temperament, was a person who was well known in the cultural circles of Sarajevo. He was very present in the cultural life of Sarajevo and well known. He was always involved in the theatre life, the university life, and so on and so forth. If I understood your question well, you wanted me to compare the two of them with Mr. Krajisnik. I can say that he was not as well known as the -- those two. He was a manager, he was an economist, and he was known only to a narrow circle of professionals and executives of his peers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: By the time we get to the end of 1990 -- no, I'll take it on in time. A year on, so by the time we get to October 1991, what was the relative standing between Mr. Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic, and Mr. Krajisnik in the eyes of the general public in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: One could say that as early as then these public positions had been distributed among these three people that you mentioned. The position of the speaker of the parliament won Mr. Krajisnik a lot of popularity. As the speaker of the parliament, he was always present in the media, and as such he became very popular in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The sessions were very frequent, they lasted very long, and media covered them quite closely. And as he chaired that body, he was always in the spotlight and always in the eyes of the viewers. Mr. Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic, on the other hand, were in more important positions, but those positions were in the shadow. They were not so much in the spotlight. As I've already said, their work was not as transparent as Mr. Krajisnik's work, and the public would be given only the conclusions of the sessions of their body. Those sessions were not open to the public. In other words, that time the situation had changed, and Mr. Krajisnik was much more present and more popular as a political figure then than the other two that we're talking about who were also members of the same party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did -- did that more prominent position, as you've described it, of Mr. Krajisnik reflect his influence within the SDS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't object when there was a question about the witness's sense or impression of what the general public knew, but I was left with the impression that this witness was closely affiliated with and a member of the Alliance of Reformists, not the SDS, and I'm wondering precisely what the basis is to ask him what Mr. Krajisnik's power was within the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the basis is for the witness to tell us if he knows the answer to the question, to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll put the question again, Mr. Kecmanovic. Did that more prominent position of Mr. Krajisnik, as you've described it, reflect his influence within the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether there is -- a result of that was more or less influence in the SDS. I can't be a judge of that. What I was talking about referred only to his public presence and popularity. He had become a media figure who was well known to everybody, not only to the Serbian people but to the other two peoples. People liked his style, liked the way he chaired the meetings of parliament. Whether this had any impact on his position within the SDS and what that impact was, I really wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. If I may add to what I just said. Mr. Karadzic was a person without any state position and still he was the leading personality in the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there in those latter months of 1990 and throughout 1991, was there apparently any rival or threat to Mr. Karadzic as the leading personality in the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think that Mr. Karadzic was by far the number one person of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you, after the 1990 elections, the rest of that year and in 1991 take part in any formal or informal meetings with leaders of other parties?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you give the Trial Chamber an idea of the nature and frequency of such meetings?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: There were both formal and informal meetings. I've already mentioned that as regards all three ethnic sides, and they were the power in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, I knew the actual individuals involved very well. These communications were informal. There were such meetings as well. However, there were also official meetings. One of these regular meetings that were held from time to time, but regularly, were meetings of the heads of the parliamentary parties within the Assembly. It was customary before parliament would meet that the speaker of the parliament would convene a preparatory meeting among the heads of the parliamentary clubs and the leaders of all parliamentary parties. I was one of persons invited to such meetings, as head of the Reformists, and that is how I met Mr. Krajisnik in an official capacity on a regular basis. There were also the representatives of the Croatian Democratic Union and the Party of Democratic Action, and also other opposition parties that had their own MPs in parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, just go back for a moment to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina after the November 1990 elections. The person who got the most votes overall was in fact Mr. Abdic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it expected at that point that he would become the president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was not only that he -- that it was expected that he would become president, but according to the rules that were set before the elections, that's the way it was supposed to be. The rules made it incumbent that the first presiding member over a one-year term should be that member of the Presidency who would win the largest number of votes in the election itself, regardless of who this may be. So according to the rules, the previously set rules, it was Fikret Abdic who was supposed to be the first president of the Presidency, and then afterwards, of course according to ethnic parity, it would be changed, rotated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But in fact, Mr. Izetbegovic became the president of the Presidency, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that, first of all, the Party of Democratic Action had a problem because this top office in Bosnia-Herzegovina was supposed to be held by a person who was not the party leader at the same time. In addition to that, Mr. Abdic was not - how should I put this? - a veteran in the Party of Democratic Action. He joined the party ranks -- or, rather, the party won him over as a man who was very popular, and it was known in advance that he would be a man who would bring in a lot of votes. That turned out to be true in the election itself. However, that turned out to be a problem for the party, especially for Izetbegovic, that the top office in the land would be won by somebody who was not he himself and not someone who is considered to be a natural member of his party. That is one aspect. Another aspect is that the Serb and Croat sides agreed to that, because had they insisted on observing the previously set rules, Izetbegovic or the Party of Democratic Action could not have changed that particular rule. However, I think that Abdic was less acceptable for them, too, less acceptable than Izetbegovic, because it was considered that Fikret Abdic was a man who had a communist inclination, that he was inclined towards communist ideology. He was a member of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, a man who in his economic enterprises showed a lot of his Bolshevik style of doing business. Market principles were not really taken into account. He counted on the support of the authorities of the state. As a matter of fact, even procedures that were not exactly legal in terms of obtaining credit and things like that. Also, that is why he was not liked very much on the outside too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, can I turn to the Croat members of the Presidency briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, before doing so, could you ask or could the witness tell us, when he says -- when he tells us about the rules that would designate Mr. Abdic to become the president of the Presidency, were these informally agreed rules? Were they put on paper? Could you give us some information about the status of those rules.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were official rules, quite official, that were publicly promulgated before the elections were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you saying it was part of electoral law?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And nevertheless, one could deviate from them, as I understand, with the agreement of all the parties, if that was part of law. Could you explain to us how that functioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. Well, I can just confirm what you've just said. The rules were official and made public and part of the electoral law. However, since this rule pertained to the Presidency and it had to do with the Presidency, the collective head of state, and who would be the first one to become the first among equals, primus inter pares. So they could agree amongst themselves. I personally feel that they were not supposed to do that, and there were objections raised in the press as well as this was a violation of the law. However, since all three parties in the Presidency agreed to this, then it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just a turn briefly to be made to the Croat members of the Presidency, who were Mr. Kljuic and Mr. Boras after the 1990 election. Were those two the most influential people in the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: It could be said that first of all the two of them did not have the same kind of influence in the HDZ. And there is something I could add to that; that there was a third man who carried more weight in the HDZ, more than either of the two, and that was Mate Boban, who was in Western Herzegovina. So he was not in Sarajevo. And actually, he was the eminence grise of the HDZ, and formally he would become the leader of the party later. As for Kljuic and Boras, Boras was a man who was closer to Boban politically and therefore he carried more weight. Whereas Kljuic, in a formal sense was for, a certain period of time, the president of the HDZ. As he worked in Sarajevo and as he pursued a line that was closer to the SDA, he enjoyed greater popularity among the Muslim population, later the Bosniak population, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was he correspondingly popular with the Croat population in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: To a lesser degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And by comparison with Boban, what was his popularity among the Croat population in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In comparison with Boban, well, I primarily meant Boban, because that was the so-called Herzegovina line in the HDZ, which actually throughout the elections and after the elections and during the war was dominant in the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the -- in --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting. Boban was the leader of that line precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in summary, perhaps at least in the first place, what was the Herzegovina line?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Herzegovina line and the HDZ insisted on, to put it in the simplest possible terms, the policy of Herceg-Bosna, a Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, on establishing a separate entity of the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, with the idea of becoming independent, linking themselves up to Croatia, or remaining within Bosnia-Herzegovina as a separate entity, territorial -- in territorial terms and also in terms of political self-government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Kljuic was against that line, was he?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic was -- well, you cannot put it that way, directly against that line. There weren't any conflicts between those two factions in the HDZ out in the open. But at any rate, he was inclined towards a solution that would be a single Bosnia-Herzegovina, a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is why the Muslim or, rather, the Bosniak people preferred him, and that's why he was also preferred by the Bosniak representatives in the Presidency, especially Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there a point at which Mr. Kljuic's influence and standing declined?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The influence of Mr. Kljuic, in view of the balance of power, was never a major one, because he didn't really have the Croat people behind him. The sympathies of the Muslim representatives were, after all, sympathies towards a potential partner, not a person who was a member of their party, their people, et cetera. This would later come to the fore when Mr. Kljuic was first replaced as leader of the HDZ. And afterwards, he was even removed from the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina through the agreement reached by Izetbegovic and the leaders of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. So his political line was on the decline; his political line, his political position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, after the 1990 elections, was there a provision in the Bosnia and Herzegovina constitution for something -- it goes under various names in English, but I'll call it in English the Council for Ethnic Equality. Perhaps you could confirm that you're receiving as the translation in your own language the name of a body that you recognise or are familiar with.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The idea of the Council of Peoples was something that was present in the minds of the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina considerably before that too. It was a multi-ethnic community with three constituent peoples, and it was considered only natural that in a democratic constellation these positions should be safeguarded. The idea about something like this was present even in the old system, and that is why, through the constitutional amendments, the communist government introduced a body called the Council for Ethnic Equality, a kind of a substitute for a proper Council or Chamber of Peoples. It was a mechanism which was of a specific nature. For want of a proper Council of Peoples, it was supposed to play the role that is played nowadays in Bosnia-Herzegovina, since Dayton, that is. It was a specific mechanism according to which, if one of the sides in the tripartite partnership in Bosnia-Herzegovina in parliament during the sitting of parliament would assess that something that is on the agenda could affect the ethnic national interest of one of the three peoples, they could intervene with the parliament, the speaker of the parliament, in writing with at least 20 signatures of MPs, and ask that they remove that from the agenda. The mechanism envisaged that then this should be sent on to a multi-ethnic commission in which all three national parties would have the right of veto. If any side would put a veto on that item of the agenda, it could no longer be returned to the agenda of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there a time after the November 1990 elections when such a procedure did operate in practice?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And during what period and in what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: This happened during that one year between the multi-party elections and the beginning of war. I think that this mechanism was used twice involving 20 signatures of MPs, and I think this mechanism functioned well, or it proved to be functional in realistic terms. I cannot remember exactly what the subject involved was, but at any rate, it had to do with ethnic equality. And that is the sole reason why this mechanism was instituted; in order to safeguard an equality of rights for all ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it correct that on a couple of occasions the mechanism operated in a practical short circuit way in the sense that, knowing that there was inevitably going to be a veto if there was a reference to this body, the proposers of the measure didn't insist on it going to that body only to get sent back following a veto?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's an interesting point, that actually the body that is called the Council for Ethnic Equality was never constituted but, in spite of that, it did carry out its function. The very fact that there would be an objection by 20 MPs from one of the national clubs would be sufficient announcement to the effect that there would be a veto at the Council for Ethnic Equality. It would not have been difficult to assume that. So that is why if there was an objection in writing by 20 MPs, that was considered to be a fait accompli. It was no longer necessary to go further up to this body where the veto would actually be made. So 20 signatures of MPs was considered to be a sufficient veto, so to speak, because further procedure would only involve repetition. Nothing would really be changed, and nothing would become stronger if it went further up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kecmanovic, we've had quite a lot of evidence in this case about the events in the Assembly on the night of the 14th and 15th of October, 1991. First of all, were you present at that Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it right that there was -- there was an attempt by Serb deputies to operate this mechanism of 20 signatures and a proposal to pursue sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina to be sent off to the Council for National Equality but that attempt turned out to be unsuccessful?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And how would you describe Mr. Krajisnik's actions and conduct as president of the Assembly in relation to that issue at that session in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that Mr. Krajisnik behaved the same way he did when chairing parliament until then, as far as I know; with a lot of patience, trying to defer matters, to avoid any kind of dramatic decisions, that breaks be taken with a view to a possible solution of the crisis and bridging the disagreement between the two parties. However, Izetbegovic -- but then I cannot say all of the SDA, because among the officials of the SDA there were politicians who during the course of that dramatic session showed more of a willingness and readiness to reach a compromise than Izetbegovic himself. A few times when it seemed that things would not only be deferred but actually resolved at the session itself, Izetbegovic came out with a very hard-line position that a decision had to be made precisely then and that there could be no postponement or deferment. Finally, Mr. Krajisnik read the request of 20 MPs of the Serb Democratic Party that the item be removed from the agenda. However, the Party of Democratic Action and its deputies and the deputies of the HDZ refused to accept that. Mr. Krajisnik, bearing in mind the necessary procedure and following the required procedure, made public the intervention of the 20 deputies - that was his duty - and he said that this infringed on ethnic equality. Since all other means were exhausted, he adjourned the session late in the evening. However, the vice-president, the vice-speaker of the Assembly, Mr. Mariofil Ljubic from the HDZ, called upon the deputies of the HDZ and the SDA to stay on. Since they had a majority, they were to reach such a decision without the presence of the Serb deputies. May I also add that this led to a rift between the opposition parties, inter alia in the party that I led, precisely along ethnic lines. Deputies of Muslim ethnicity stayed on -- some of them stayed on and supported the position of Alija Izetbegovic, whereas the Serbs among these MPs, including myself, although I was head of the party, not an MP, we left the session, believing that this is a very dangerous decision and a decision that of course does not honour the equality of rights of all three peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the constituent peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the state-forming peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, we heard plenty of evidence about this, Mr. Kecmanovic. One of the important reactions to these events was the founding of the Serb Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you personally attend the founding session of that Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian Democratic Party, which scheduled its founding meeting, sent out invitations to the heads of other political parties. Amongst other people, one invitation came to me, but also invitations were sent to some people from the -- from everyday life, people who did not belong to any political parties. Amongst others, I responded to that invitation, and I attended the founding session of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you personally attend any subsequent sessions of the Serb Assembly or what became the Assembly of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. This was the founding session, and it had a very specific nature. It was a ceremonial meeting, not a working meeting. There were representatives of other peoples, of other parties. That's why it was so special in nature. The subsequent sessions of the Serbian Assembly were working meetings. Therefore, I was neither invited nor did I attend any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, just looking at your own party at that time, you've described to the Trial Chamber a different reaction on the night of October 14th and 15th from some Muslim members of your party as opposed to Serb members. Were those differences repaired or did they cause changes within your own party?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: This resulted in a crisis in the party. Up to then, there was a high degree of homogeneity in the party, especially when we're talking about the inner leadership that counted some 20 to 30 members. This was a body which was called Presidency. It had very frequent sessions, and it was mostly composed of people who resided in Sarajevo, which enabled them frequent contacts. There was a high degree of closeness among these people based on their previous acquaintance, on the continuity of their previous work. Together in the leadership we fostered openness to various ethnicities. We believed that our multi-ethnic composition enabled us to talk in the way in which the ruling coalition talked amongst different parties. However, this was a dramatic decision, this vote was a dramatic vote which seriously shook the party. Some people left it because they could not forgive their peers for having voted the way they did. The others had misgivings because people didn't -- didn't vote as they wanted them to vote. To cut a long story short, quite a lot of members left the party after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did your party adopt or retain a clear policy in relation to the issue of sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina after that Assembly session on October 14th, 15th?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Our position was under the influence of all these events, and I have to say that the fact that there was quite a decrease in the number of our membership, our position was that none of the mono-ethnic parties in the ruling coalition should not take unilateral moves without a prior consensus of all the three constituent peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The position of the party in principle was against such a decision, like it was for -- against any unilateral move on the part of any of the three mono-ethnic parties. Or if you will, indirectly we condemned that thing that happened in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There seem -- please explain if this is wrong: There seem to be two separate elements there, Mr. Kecmanovic: First of all, your party, from what you've said, was against the fact that such a decision had been put through the Assembly by the Muslim-Croat coalition in the face of Serb opposition. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. There was another additional argument when it came to our party. As I've already mentioned, our party was a Yugoslav party. In general terms, we were in favour of the preservation of Yugoslavia. The decision that was made during that dramatic night in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a decision on the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Yugoslavia. This was something that was contrary to our programme, to the principles that our party was based on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Our name, our integral name, was the Alliance of Reformist Forces of Yugoslavia for Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was our full title. The secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Yugoslav framework was contrary to the concept of our party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did your party adopt a public position in relation to the establishment of the Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think that this was perceived as an integral part of the story that took place in the joint Assembly in Sarajevo, that this was nothing more but a consequence. One side was out-voted and, as a result of that, it was no longer prepared to cooperate in joint Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did -- in the first place ask about you personally, Mr. Kecmanovic, your own position in the party, did you adopt a position out of the public eye in relation to the establishment of the Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I'm not sure, but I don't think so. You have to bear in mind that under such position, the position of the leader of a multi-ethnic party was already rather complicated. One had to juggle amongst the three ethnic interests which became prominent within that multi-ethnically-based party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you view the establishment of the Serb Assembly as an unreasonable response to the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, because I perceived this more as a warning, as an ultimatum. Proof that this was not interruption of the communication and that it was not the final act of the drama was the fact that Mr. Krajisnik remained the speaker of the joint Assembly. He was both the president of the Serbian Assembly as well as the speaker of the joint Assembly. How shall I put it? I think that he maintained this link and the hand remained extended through him for a future reconstruction of the joint Assembly. In other words, after this incident, given the adequate condition, this joint Assembly could still go on working. That door was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had leading members of your own party left your party? Did they quite soon after the 14th, 15th of October?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Some did. Some left the party and its leadership, but as a result of that there was an even larger decrease in the number of our members.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What -- what sort of size membership did your party have immediately before the Assembly session on the 14th, 15th October 1991?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you give us some idea of the scale of membership?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have a perception. After we lost the elections; i.e., after we had such poor results during the elections, there was a decrease in the number of our members. You have to bear in mind this didn't happen only to the Reformists but also to many other parties that had been established prior to the elections. Those were not parties with a long tradition based on which they would enjoy a greater loyalty of their members. Those parties were ad hoc parties that were established on the eve of the multi-party elections. So the degree of loyalty was very low, especially in the case of those parties that won the elections. The only exception was the former League of Communists, which had a long continuity, and although its membership dwindled down, there were still people loyal to that party and remained with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've reached a break in topics, if that were convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's at the same time a convenient moment to have a break. We'll adjourn until ten minutes past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, I made a mistake by asking you to already enter to the courtroom, because I need two minutes to deal with a procedural matter which has, to some extent, nothing to do with you, and to the extent it has, should not be said in your presence. So could I ask you - it will not take more than two minutes - to leave the courtroom. And I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you asked to get an opportunity to address the Chamber in view of the filing of final briefs. We do that at the end of the three witnesses we have -- we are now hearing, so that would be on the 11th of April. And if we would find no time on the 11th of April, then it's something you can do just prior to the beginning of the evidence of Mr. Krajisnik. That's the first issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Talking about the 11th of April and looking at the scheduling for the days to come, the Chamber is again concerned on whether we'll be able to finish as scheduled on the 10th of April, as a matter of fact, although some overflow possible until the 11th of April. I can't do anything else than to express this concern and add to that, and that's in relation with this witness, that looking at the last one hour and a half, the Chamber, I think out of the one and a half hours, if there was 20 minutes of new, fresh evidence, it -- it's already a positive estimate. I mean, the Chamber is aware and has heard quite some evidence on matters like those who wanted to stay in the former Yugoslavia were blocking a decision by a majority to get out of the former Yugoslavia, just as those who wanted to get out of the former Yugoslavia, by the majority out-voted the minority. We have gone over that again and again, and I do not think - and I'm addressing you Mr. Tieger - that this is something really in dispute, or is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm -- I would be hard pressed to identify, at least at this point, the differences between the evidence the Court just referred to and the evidence that was led by the Prosecution during the course of its case about these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's more or less the function of this -- of this constitutional -- what was it? It was not committee although sometimes called Committee on Equality -- Council for the Ethnical Equality. I mean, it's -- it's so clear that you're -- that a deadlock will easily result if one minority in such a council could block, by having 20 votes in the Assembly, to block any further decision-taking which would be in accordance with the majority, just as the majority might have felt frustrated -- just as the -- this minority, having felt frustrated if not using that instrument that they would be out-voted in the Assembly. That structure, which we spent, again, so much time on it, and then looking at the 10th or 11th of April, Mr. Stewart, the Chamber really wonders whether it would not have been possible that the -- I would say that what the witness adds to it could not have been presented more efficiently and more quickly. And the second issue is that the Chamber wondered whether the position of the party this witness belonged to should be dealt with in so much detail. What I can add to that, there's no way for this Chamber to proceed, also for practical reasons, beyond the 11th of April. So the 11th of April is -- is really the last day. Tuesday, the 11th of April. Just asking your attention for it. And I'd like to ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just -- perhaps it might be helpful if I just indicate -- Well, first of all, Your Honour, I say straight away this is not one of those occasions where I'm going to suggest that there's nothing in what Your Honour has just said. So I take -- I take some of the points Your Honour has made, and I'm not -- I'm not proposing, having, if you like, had a sort of introductory session with this witness, I'm not proposing to go over all sorts of extraneous detail, but -- I won't spend time going into what we've already heard, Your Honour, but I take the point. But looking ahead to the witnesses, we have, in our discussions and our planning, we have taken it that, as Your Honours have indicated, that the 11th is the last day of this current run of hearing witnesses. Your Honour, we have this witness, the next witness, who has been brought here, as Your Honour knows and who is here, and then we have the witness for whom there is an application for protective measures. Your Honour, we can't see any way in which any more witnesses than those can be fitted in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the Chamber is concerned on whether we could finish those witnesses within the time still available.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's what I'm coming to, Your Honour. We are proceeding on the basis that we expect to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But can I say straight away Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- that this, well, directly affects Mr. Josse, because he will be taking the next witness, that preparation for the next witness presents its difficulties in this sense, that it's really, from a practical point of view, not going to be possible for Mr. Josse to present that witness to start before Thursday, Your Honour. So that does -- if there is -- I don't know whether there will be, but if there is a gap between the end of this current witness and the beginning of that witness, Your Honour, I do know from discussion with Mr. Josse it's not a gap that it's fair to ask Mr. Josse to plug by having that witness ready to begin evidence on Wednesday. But, Your Honour, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's even --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- calculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then again even more time not available in court and we really wonder how you'll manage to do it, but it's finally -- it's your responsibility, and I -- well, my observations I just made are, I would say, for this very moment sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the squeeze is going to come on that last witness, in effect, Your Honour, but we accept that we must -- we must fit that last witness in in the time that the Court is making available, and we acknowledge that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Kecmanovic to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Kecmanovic. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, between the end of 1991 and the end of March 1992, was there actual violence that you were aware of in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The situation in Sarajevo was very tense, but violence happened in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. For example, I remember in Sijekovac there was an incident. The state Presidency; i.e., several members of the Presidency, were sent there to calm the situation down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But in Sarajevo itself, there was no actual violence of which you were aware?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: There was violence in Sarajevo, primarily against the Serbian population, and especially against the families of JNA officers, irrespective of their status; i.e., whether they were active officers and their families or retired officers and their families. Their apartments were stormed and searched, even plundered, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you at any point in the first three months of 1992 come to the view that war was approaching the inevitable?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In that respect, I believe that the turning point was the dissolution of the parliament in Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, when the principle of equality was disrespected for the first time. It was obvious that the -- this would not be a one-off but that there was, rather, a very deep discord amongst the newly formed power. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the national parity was a prerequisite to the peace, and a dramatic violation of that principle was bound to have consequence and was bound not to -- not to be a singular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you during that period, the first three months of 1992, have any contact yourself with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that those were, first and foremost, meetings in the parliament. The speaker of the parliament called those meetings pursuant to the standing procedure in order to coordinate the work of the parties. Those were regular meetings. There were also some informal meetings, meetings which involved our personal encounters relative to my work at the university. At that time, I was the dean of the University of Sarajevo, and as such I had to be in contact with the representatives of the authorities, including Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you form any impression from your contact with Mr. Krajisnik as to any work done by him to try to avert war?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, together with all the other officials of the SDS, or the leaders of the Serbian National Party, as most of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina stood by the SDS, most of the Muslims stood by the SDA, and most of the Serb -- Croats stood by the HDZ. So Mr. Krajisnik was the first amongst the leaders of this national movement who was best accepted by the other two parties as an interlocutor. He had a ritual which in my eyes looked a bit unnecessary, and I would sometimes make jokes at his expense. At the beginning of such meetings, he would often tell us a story about his family and about his finding his place in his multi-ethnic midst. He told us that his father always told him -- and Mr. Krajisnik would address Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Kljuic -- he said that his father always told him how important neighbourly relations were, but there was always an accompanying remark. His father always told him to respect his neighbours, and if he had to do something at the expense of any of the neighbours, then he should do it at the expense of a Serb rather than a Croat or a Muslim because the consequences would be lesser. This was his staple introduction to any of those meetings, and as I often sat next to him, I would often ask him whether he would open the meeting with the same story, because if he was, I would go out and have a cigarette and then come back. He would tell me that his story is very important and that it should be repeated in -- because of the good inter-ethnic relationship. And although he repeated the story again and again, it always met with the understanding of all the participants in the meeting. Mr. Krajisnik was the best loved negotiator on the Serbian side when it came to negotiations with the other parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, may I stop you here. We are under considerable time restraints. It took you four minutes to explain in quite some detail how Mr. Krajisnik - and that's the core of your answer - always stressed the importance of good relationship, inter-ethnic relationship, with your neighbours, and he did not cease to emphasise that, which he learned already from his father, as he told us. Now, it took me approximately half a minute to say this. It took you four minutes. And the question was -- I think a very important question. The question was whether you formed an impression from your contact with Mr. Krajisnik as to any work done by him to try to avert war. So could you please -- I'm not obstructing you from telling what you told us, I'm asking you to do that in 20 to 30 seconds and then come to the core of the question. So tell us whether you formed an impression on any work done by Mr. Krajisnik to avert war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember any specific sentence or specific words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you recall any actions --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I can just remind you of something that I said before the break, and that is that he was the only official amongst the Serbian top leadership who kept his position. He remained the speaker of the joint Assembly, whereas Koljevic and Plavsic withdrew from the Presidency. And I understand this as a gesture of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's -- just to be clear, it's -- Koljevic and Plavsic withdrew from the Presidency in April 1992. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that was specifically following the call by Mr. Izetbegovic for mobilisation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Even after that Mr. Krajisnik remained in his position as the speaker of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: During those first three months that I asked you about, January to March 1992, did -- were you aware of any actions by Mr. Krajisnik that tended to provoke or increase the risk of war?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you -- did you ever hear in the whole of that period, 1991, 1992 - and I'll embrace the whole of 1992 - did you ever hear of something called Variants A and B?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Before we proceed further, to come back to a sentence uttered by -- the witness said, and I haven't -- clarify. I'm not sure whether I understood the meaning properly. You said that: "[In English] ... I believe that the turning point was the dissolution of the parliament in Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, when the principle of equality was disrespected for the first time. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the national parity was a prerequisite to the peace, and a dramatic violation of that principle was bound to have consequence ..." [Interpretation] So could you clarify that sentence for us? Could you tell me exactly what you mean by all this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a nutshell, I believe that the vote in favour of the referendum against the will of the Serbian representatives in Bosnia-Herzegovina was a decisive step that eventually resulted in the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Again, during the whole of 1991 and 1992, did you ever hear of something called the six strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You were familiar, were you, with the Cutileiro talks and the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Not only did I know, but I also attended some meetings which were chaired by Cutileiro in Sarajevo. I was even supposed to go to Lisbon to the last session that ended on a sour note, however, due to technical circumstances and delays, I did not go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you supportive of the -- such agreements as were made pursuant to the Cutileiro discussions?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was the sour note that you referred to a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I primarily referred to the fact that although the three parties were on the verge of reaching an agreement on the solution to the crisis, and the three leaders signed the agreement, however, one of the sides withdrew from the agreement. In more specific terms, it was Mr. Izetbegovic who finally decided not to put his signature on the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you -- were you ever aware of anything which signified that the SDS leadership were not genuinely committed to the Cutileiro Plan if others had supported it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this in dispute, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This witness's awareness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If let's say if Mr. Izetbegovic would not have withdrawn, is the position of the Prosecution that the SDS would not have committed itself to the Cutileiro agreement or not the full agreement at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The Prosecution has led no evidence to that effect and has not relied on any proposition to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, of course this Chamber has not proofed the witness, but the sour note, I would have betted - good English tradition, isn't it - for 95 per cent that it would be the withdrawal of Mr. Izetbegovic, which we've heard some 20 times. Of course if you would have expected anything else, certainly it would have been a question to ask more specifically about the sour note. If, however, he would have expected the same, after briefing this witness, the question was totally superfluous. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Sometimes I have to assess what gambles I will or won't take on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf, and perhaps I got that one wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Kecmanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry to interrupt Mr. Stewart. If witness can take off his earphones, I want to clarify that answer so there is no misunderstanding about the Cutileiro Plan vis-a-vis the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kecmanovic, first of all, do you understand any English? You do. It wouldn't help, Mr. Tieger. Can we leave it? I mean, at this moment it seems not to be an urgent matter. Can we leave that for the very end of this session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will keep it in mind, I take it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll write it down and keep it in front of me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, it may not be a matter of scientific definition, but when do you regard the war as having started?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can mention a few events that, on a cumulative basis, made up something that would be called the beginning of the war. Actually, it was the occupation of JNA barracks in the city of Sarajevo, because the army, the JNA, in Sarajevo played a very useful role, because it intervened neutrally in the conflicts among the three sides. I'm referring to the so-called Serb barricades or roadblocks. Although in that stage, after Slovenia and Croatia had left, the JNA consisted primarily of Serb officers and soldiers, but the JNA intervened against barricades that were put up by the Serb side in certain parts of town after a member of a Serb wedding party was killed, Gardovic. That showed that the army had a neutral position towards all three sides irrespective of its ethnic composition. However, in spite of that, at one point in time the JNA barracks were occupied, or surrounded, which means that part of the Sarajevo population had a hostile attitude towards the JNA. So this was something that caused concern and a great deal of anxiety among the population in Sarajevo. Another thing that I could note from this period in time was that one night there was a showdown in the town of Sarajevo in the late-night hours. There was gunfire and it was hard to establish what this was all about. However, the next day when I went out into the street, all the shops in the centre of the city had been demolished. Nothing was left in them, which means that there was a kind of showdown within the town itself among paramilitary gangs. It wasn't clear among who, but at any rate, it was an indicator that organs of government no longer functioned in Sarajevo and that they could not keep elementary law and order. And that was an indicator for me that the situation was worsening dramatically.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you became aware, did you, that at some point in April 1992 the SDS leadership, including Mr. Krajisnik, left Sarajevo and moved to Pale?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was under special circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what you just described a moment ago about a showdown in Sarajevo and gunfire and so on, those events occurred before that departure of the SDS leadership to Pale, did they?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you -- at some point after the SDS leaders had gone to Pale, were you instrumental in arranging a meeting between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First of all, can you say when -- we'll come to the arrangement of the meeting in a moment. First of all, can you say when the meeting occurred?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in the month of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And where did the meeting occur?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't heard you. I haven't heard the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where did the meeting occur?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: One meeting was in late April, I think, at Ilidza at the Terme Hotel, and the other one was in Lukavica. These were my meetings with Krajisnik along with Mirko Pejanovic. And there was also a meeting when I organised talks between Krajisnik and Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, can we first of all, please, just get them in their correct chronological sequence. You've referred to three meetings. You referred to them in the order of a meeting at the Terme Hotel, a meeting at Lukavica, and another meeting between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Izetbegovic. What's the chronological order of those three meetings?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The first meeting was at the Terme Hotel in Ilidza. The second one was the meeting that I organised between Izetbegovic and Krajisnik, and the third one was with Krajisnik in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I want to ask you about them in the chronological order in which you've told the Trial Chamber they occurred. So the meeting at the Terme Hotel, first of all, as accurately as you can remember, when did that take place?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in the month of April. And the meeting was also attended by Mr. Mirko Pejanovic, who later became a member of the Presidency with me. He was a candidate of the Socialist Party of the presidential elections. And at the meeting at Terme Hotel, Mr. Krajisnik was -- Mr. Karadzic was also present in addition to Mr. Krajisnik. So four participants altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. Can I just -- first of all, how did that meeting come about?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That meeting was held at my initiative, and Mirko Pejanovic's too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: As party leaders, we wanted to see Karadzic and Krajisnik, and quite simply to get information about the situation. We knew about it from the inside, but we wanted to see what it was like from the outside once this separation line had already been established, slowly but surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the separation line being where?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The separation line was still rather undefined. Quite simply, there weren't any formal obstacles yet, but the population concentrated on two sides, and at that time we could still take a taxi in order to go to that meeting. Of course it wasn't easy to find a taxi driver who was ready to drive there, but it wasn't too difficult either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
