utterances.text: And were you able to obtain useful information at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing spectacular. It was just more complete information about the situation being -- the situation being very bad, increasingly difficult, with less and less hope of agreement being reached among the different sides, and that was about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did the whole meeting -- how long did the meeting last?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Half an hour to one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were the four of you active participants in the whole of the meeting during that period?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But Radovan Karadzic came to the meeting a bit later, and I think he had some interview for television or newspapers, so he had to leave the meeting early too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was -- was anything discussed at that meeting by way of plans or proposals that might achieve peace?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing specific. Everybody expressed great concern over the situation that was very serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did anything of value come out of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. It didn't have that kind of ambition either. Since we both led multi-ethnic parties and we were ethnic Serbs, the assumption was that we could communicate more easily and in a more relaxed manner with the leaders of the SDS than people who were, say, ethnic Croats or Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it -- was it you and Mr. Pejanovic who had asked specifically for Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik to attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It was at our initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Why had you asked for Mr. Krajisnik to be at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Our request was not very specific, as far as I can remember. We simply asked to see some people from the Serb leadership. I have to repeat this: We all knew each other very well from earlier on. It could have been the late Koljevic or somebody else. The point of our meeting would have achieved that -- would have been achieved that way too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, the meeting that you -- the next one that you placed in the chronological sequence, the meeting between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Izetbegovic, how did that meeting come about?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That meeting came about at my initiative. I think that I had consulted the members of the leadership of my party about it too. Quite simply, the motive was - in view of the fact that a war was already on - to do something again in order to stop the clashes around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, to stop the clashes around Sarajevo or, a wider ambition, to stop the fighting around Bosnia -- the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Primarily it had to do with Sarajevo, because we in town did not have any specific information at that time as to what was going on throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. Among other things, we thought that the position of the capital city is of particular significance in terms of peace initiatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Izetbegovic was plainly the leader on the Muslim side, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the reason for setting up this meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic on the one hand and Mr. Krajisnik on the other?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: This initiative was first launched vis-a-vis Izetbegovic. Izetbegovic wanted Mr. Krajisnik to be his collocutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did he indicate why?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: As he had put it -- well, it wasn't necessary for anybody to say anything, but it went without saying that he was the favourite Serb interlocutor as far as Muslims were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And for what reason was he their favourite?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Because he always left the impression of a calm man, a patient negotiator, a man who always tried to build bridges or to keep bridges, bridges that had become shaky, if I can put it that way. Mr. Krajisnik usually would not raise his voice or quarrel or present things rigidly. In parliament, he proved to be very patient, tactical -- rather, tactful, and I think that that is what made him get such standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, the -- what -- what time of day did the meeting occur?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were you present?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So Mr. Krajisnik was present, Mr. Izetbegovic was present, you were present; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Anybody else present?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And -- well, what -- what was the discussion?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The subject of the meeting was what I had already mentioned; that is to say, how to stop the war conflicts in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did anybody present come up with any concrete proposals as to how to do that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In a way, I had proposed the subject to both sides and that was accepted. Now the question was how to carry this through. Mr. Krajisnik mentioned the idea that it would be necessary to have some temporary separation in order to pacify the front line, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Temporary separation in what sense?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik insisted on this being temporary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. What -- separation of what from what, in what way?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Quite simply by taking the population concentrations that had been established as a given situation, a temporary situation, though, that should be pacified. You see, the town was already separated. There was a front line. Mr. Krajisnik suggested to proceed from the actual state of affairs to freeze it temporarily so that the conflicts would cease.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And at what -- what, then, was the practical result proposed to be? Temporary, albeit.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that did not happen, so we can only speak in the conditional. What the result was supposed to be was to have a cease-fire, because both sides wanted to advance in territorial terms in that situation. So if there were to be a freeze on the situation as it was, that should have brought about a pacification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Izetbegovic's reaction to Mr. Krajisnik's suggestion?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: At first he expressed some reservations regarding that, and then at the insistence of Mr. Krajisnik that this was a temporary situation and that the sole objective was to stop the conflicts and that this was a temporary situation and that he was sure that he and Izetbegovic would live to see an overcoming of the war situation and that the previous situation would be re-established, that is to say without the separations, so after that, Izetbegovic accepted the proposal, and then the situation that cropped up was how to carry this out in technical terms, so to speak. Krajisnik offered Izetbegovic that he should give a kind of proposal in this regard. However, Izetbegovic replied that Krajisnik should do it. So after a few reciprocal suggestions of this kind - you do it; you do it, and so on - I said that it would be most logical to formulate certain proposals in an operative sense, that they should be put on paper and that then we meet again and continue our discussion. And then one of them - either one or the other, I cannot remember - thought of me being the one who was to make the proposals about the alternatives. So at their request I accepted that, and it was agreed that I put this on paper, a few options, and that we meet again the following day at the same time, again at midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you then put some options on paper?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did that, as agreed. And also as agreed, I sent these options to Pale by fax, and I received an affirmative answer. Namely, the Serb side accepted option number 4. And then I went to the Presidency and I gave the same paper to Izetbegovic. And it's interesting to note that after looking at the proposal briefly, he chose the same option, option number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it -- do you know, was it Mr. Krajisnik who had responded to your fax to -- fax or faxes to Pale and notifying acceptance of option number 4?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The late Mr. Koljevic phoned me and said that option number 4 was acceptable to him, and then I asked him whether that was only his position or the position of the leadership. Was Karadzic involved, I asked. And he said that he talked to Karadzic and that this is actually the position of the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- since the Bosnian Serbs had chosen the same proposal as Mr. Izetbegovic, was it then implemented?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In this way I had done my part of the job practically. I was sitting in President Izetbegovic's office when Mr. Krajisnik telephoned Mr. Izetbegovic. I think, as far as I understood things, was that the only problem was that on the previous night Mr. Krajisnik's car had been shot at by the Muslim side, and therefore he asked for the second round of negotiations to take place on the Serb side, because the first was on the Muslim side. I did not follow matters further because I thought that I had completed my mission as an intermediary, and I left Izetbegovic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know whether they, Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Krajisnik, did in fact meet the following day, or night?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know at all what follow-up, if any, there was after that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I really don't know. As a matter of fact, I wasn't really interested in it later, because you see, the situation was such that things were happening very fast. I thought that I did what I could have done, and I informed my colleagues in my party about it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the meeting you've just described with the three of you there, was there any discussion about a conflict in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Other than Sarajevo, that is.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The meeting between Krajisnik and Izetbegovic was very cordial, with a lot of private questions about the respective wives and families and children. I was the one who wanted to move on. And the topic was Sarajevo and there was no discussion about the situation in the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you able to give any useful indication as to how long after the Bosnian Serb leadership moved to Pale this meeting between Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Krajisnik took place?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that this was in May, but maybe towards the end of April, beginning of May, maybe around the 28th or the 30th of April, if my memory serves me well, but I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the third of the meetings that you mentioned a little while ago, the one that took place at Lukavica, how long after the Krajisnik-Izetbegovic meeting did that take place?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The third meeting that you are mentioning now, the meeting in Lukavica, must have been towards the end of May. This meeting was also dedicated to my appointment to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was in the first half of June. So this must have been towards the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was the purpose, then, of the meeting -- well, no. First of all, who did -- how was the meeting in Lukavica set up? Who took the initiative, if anybody, for that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mirko Pejanovic and I did that. We established communication. We got in touch with Pale through Mr. Krajisnik's brother whose phone number we had. He was our liaison person for communication with the leadership in Pale in a very informal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you -- was your proposal -- you and Mr. Pejanovic were in complete agreement about what you wanted from this meeting and who you wanted to be there, were you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: We were supposed to fill up two empty spaces in the Presidency that belonged to the Serbs. Under the law, it was envisaged that if there were empty seats for whatever reason - health reasons, death, or something else - that there would be no by-elections but, rather, that these seats would be filled by those candidates who had won most numbers. In this case, candidates number 3 and 4. Those seats were empty because Plavsic and Koljevic had left, and we believed that it was our obligation to appear not only as the leaders of multi-ethnic parties but also Serbian representatives, and we thought that we would have to consult this leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you propose who particularly you wished to consult?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. Although the preliminary conversation was carried out by Pejanovic, and I really don't know whether he mentioned any specific names or he just asked for a contact. Mirko Pejanovic knew Momir's brother well before the war, and that's why he was in charge of their communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did the four of you meet then, Mr. Pejanovic, you -- well, who was present at that meeting at Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The three of us, not four of us; Mr. Krajisnik, Pejanovic, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: This was a meeting for which the -- the office of the president; i.e., the Presidency, provided technical support. Izetbegovic's office that was. It was necessary for us to have the consent of both sides, because it was no longer possible to cross from one side to another in a taxi. That's why we were provided with a vehicle of the Presidency. We drove through no man's land and we were met on the Serbian side from which we were taken to Lukavica, and there we met with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And there were just the three of you present throughout the meeting, were there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And how long did it last?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. In any case, less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did anything useful emerge from the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Pejanovic and I presented to Mr. Krajisnik our position as people who played by the rules and were supposed to fill up two Serbian places, although in that respect we did not have the national legitimacy. However, the procedure was in our favour, but we did not have the mandate to represent the Serbian people. And according to the structure of the Presidency, this is precisely the role that we were supposed to play.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So was -- you were raising this point. Was there a resolution or agreement about these matters?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik did not have the authority to give us support or to refrain from giving it to us. It was just our wish to inform the Serbian side on what was happening. I remember that an alternative to that was for Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic to come back to the Presidency. Not to the centre of the town, because this was not realistic, but just withdraw their resignations. This would have helped us not to have to represent the Serbian side without the legitimacy that rose from the results of the elections. Mr. Krajisnik said that he would convey our message but that they are the ones who were in a position to withdraw their resignations just like they were in a position to hand in their resignations to their membership in the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So for you and Mr. Pejanovic, did you both favour the solution of Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic withdrawing their resignations?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't claim that this was Pejanovic's position, but it was mine and this is exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did -- did Mr. Krajisnik give or purport to give you any instructions or directions in relation to the Presidency or your future actions in relation to the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I told Mr. Krajisnik that I would have a condition for which I have the support of my party and Pejanovic's support, and that condition was the introduction of a veto in the Presidency, because it was precisely the majority vote that made the positions of Plavsic and Koljevic unsustainable in the Presidency. I said that the -- that both of us would insist on that condition, and that was the only way there could be no out-voting, and it was precisely the out-voting that forced Plavsic and Koljevic out of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there discussion at that meeting about any other topic apart from what you've already related about the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, save for some very informal private matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In -- in May 1992, did you go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And at whose initiative or suggestion did you go?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: This was another initiative of mine in the party, and then it was a party initiative proposed to the Presidency; i.e., to Izetbegovic. At the time, Izetbegovic was the one who held all the strings in Sarajevo in his hands. And the initiative was about an attempt to try and resolve the status of the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to find a solution that would provide for the JNA to stay in Bosnia-Herzegovina but to respect the democratically elected Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, all the while protecting peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I proposed that to Izetbegovic. He accepted that, and he even provided us with the wording of the proposal that could be offered to the Main Staff of the JNA in Belgrade. He proposed that this should be a five-year transitory period during which the army would have the status that I have just described. And after those five years, some of the troops that had remained in Bosnia-Herzegovina could become incorporated into the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and thus become the army of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And those who didn't wish to do so could go wherever they wanted. And the third responsibility was for those who had reached the pensionable age to be retired. This was my specific proposal accepted by Izetbegovic, and it is with this proposal that I left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you go on your own or were you accompanied?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't go on my own. I insisted on being accompanied by two other members of my party. I wanted our group to be composed of the representatives of the three peoples. One of them was Sejfudin Tokic, a Croat from the leadership, and the third one was Croat Josip Pejakovic. Izetbegovic provided us with a plane. He actually offered us a plane ride. I said I didn't want to fly in the government plane but, rather, the Energoinvest plane in order to stress the informal nature of that journey and meeting in Belgrade. And he in turn asked me to talk to General Kukanjac and ask them to allow us to take off from the Sarajevo airport which was at the time under the control of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And whom did you meet in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: It had been agreed that this meeting would be with the president of Yugoslavia. Actually, the president of the Presidency, which at the time was the body that was the Supreme Commander of the army. At that time, the president of the Presidency was also the Chief of the General Staff of the JNA. Those were the meetings that had been agreed. However, on the eve of our departure, Izetbegovic asked me eyeball-to-eyeball whether I could also meet with Slobodan Milosevic, who was the President of Serbia at the time. He believed that Milosevic's support to that project was of the utmost importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, the -- the president of the Presidency at the time, was that Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Branko Kostic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Branko Kostic.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what position did General Adzic have at the time?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: General Blagoje Adzic was not the Chief of the General Staff but the minister of defence, as far as I can remember. He was either the Chief of the General Staff or a defence minister, either/or. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you meet him, General Adzic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. First we met with General Adzic, then with the president of the Presidency, Branko Kostic, and finally, with the President Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Separately -- there were three separate meetings with those three separate people, were there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was anything agreed?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In all three cases, we conveyed our proposal, and we received support. However, a question was raised as to what to do next, because those three meetings were rather informal. And then there was a proposal either by Kostic or by Adzic upon our suggestion, which was that the following stage should be taken over by a Muslim from the Presidency and that Fikret Abdic would be best suited for that because of his good business relations all over the country. Our collocutors in Belgrade accepted our proposal, and we conveyed their agreement to -- in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what -- what specifically was agreed that you conveyed back to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The formula was completed by Izetbegovic, and that was that the JNA should stay in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina as the guarantor of peace and security and also prevention of inter-ethnic clashes for a term of five years. In the meantime, the JNA was supposed to respect the position of the Presidency of the state which had been elected in a democratic and legal way, and that after five years the troops and officers would have the right to choose whether to become members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whether they would be retired, or whether they would go back to their own respective homes and become members of their respective armies there. This was the proposal that had been accepted in Belgrade, and we just conveyed the agreement of federal institutions. This initiative took from strength to strength. Izetbegovic went to Belgrade, and the final act of that agreement took place in Ohrid at the well-known Ohrid meeting attended by Izetbegovic, Kostic, Adzic, and the meeting was hosted by Kiro Gligorov.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: However, all this eventually came to nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And why did it come to nothing?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Although the agreement was reached in Ohrid, and this was made public, on his return to Sarajevo, Izetbegovic presented the agreement before the Presidency, but the Presidency refused that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, was the Bosnian Serb leadership involved in any way in those discussions and meetings in Belgrade that you've just been referring to?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you consult or did you seek the views of any of the Bosnian Serb leadership in advance of going to Belgrade or while you were in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't do that. I didn't think this to be necessary, because the Serbian side trusted the Yugoslav People's Army, and I was convinced that they would have nothing to say against an arrangement of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you report the outcome of those discussions and meetings in Belgrade subsequently to anybody in the Bosnian Serb leadership in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The results of our activities were very soon made public. As soon as we returned from Belgrade, I reported to Izetbegovic about the course of our talks, about the favourable outcome, and he asked me to inform the members of the Presidency who were waiting for my report. I did it, and after that session I know that there was a press conference and the results of our talks were made public. I also had an interview on TV in which I explained the entire initiative and -- and I informed the general public about the outcome of that initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, apart from when you were away in Belgrade, for example, you remained living, did you, throughout this period in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you lived in the city itself, in the -- centrally in the city?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: One of your children you had moved to Belgrade in March; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My son left in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And your daughter, you arranged for her to go sometime in May, did you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, my daughter was very young. After the events that I described, the shooting during the night when everything in the centre of Sarajevo was demolished and devastated, and when I realised that the basic safety was no longer in place, I sent her to Belgrade as well, to her aunt, my sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your daughter was in her mid-teens at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it possible for -- well, Mr. Kecmanovic, you were able -- because of your position, you were able more readily than the average Serb in Sarajevo to make arrangements for your family to leave, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it possible for the run of the Serb citizenry of Sarajevo to leave if they wished in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The situation got worse gradually. During the first weeks of the war, it was rather easy to do that. As I've already said, you could even take a taxi and cross from one side to another. As time went on, it became more and more difficult. I remember as I was leaving Belgrade with my colleagues from the party, it was at the airport I faced the drama of those people who were trying to leave Sarajevo. It was like in a movie, the movie Apocalypse Now when the Americans were leaving Saigon; people were trying to grab onto the wings of the aeroplane in order to leave Sarajevo. It was very difficult to do that. There were large numbers of people waiting at the Sarajevo airport to see if they would be able to leave. Day in and day out this was becoming more and more difficult. And there were people who even put their lives at stake in order to be able to leave. And they also paid a lot of money in order to be able to leave Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm looking at the clock. Time for our next break. But I also promised Mr. Tieger a second. Madam Usher, would you please be so kind to escort Mr. Kecmanovic out of the courtroom. We'll have a break for approximately 20, 25 minutes. [The witness stands down)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I don't believe there is a misunderstanding between the parties but I thought better to make certain that that was the case. The question the Court put to me about what the Prosecution disputed or not was in the context of the so-called sour note and who withdrew or backed away from the Cutileiro discussions, and as the Court noted, and specifically -- and as I acknowledged, there was considerable evidence on that previously and that's not in dispute. I don't want there to be a misunderstanding, however, about what would have happened thereafter, and some suggestion that there was a specific agreement to -- upon which any of the parties would have acted and would have implemented in accordance. So Mr. Stewart made reference to something about such agreement as there was. The Court knows, based on previous evidence, I think, what the status of the negotiations was at that time. Maybe there is a dispute about that between the parties, I don't know, but my acknowledgment was with respect to who backed away at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question by Mr. Stewart dealt with the genuine commitment, which is a -- perhaps not in every respect practically, is a commitment to sign it, to agree with it. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Based on my -- based on the state of the evidence, I would say that it's -- it's -- we don't have any argument that the Bosnian Serb side wanted to -- was prepared to move forward and the -- and that Mr. Izetbegovic seemed to back away. Beyond that, there may be more details to discuss, but I wasn't indicating anything beyond that, and I thought that's what was being asked at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I had that in my mind. Apart from that, the -- that's also what I had in my mind when I alluded to the facts that the evidence was repetitious. Apart from that, Mr. Stewart, where you said you were willing to -- you're taking -- whether or not to take risks on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf, of course the 65 ter summary says quite clearly that the witness will highlight also Izetbegovic's failure to honour signed agreements, which I understood in this context that being the Cutileiro Plan, but if I'm wrong, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not quite sure I follow that. A 65 ter summary is not the witness's evidence, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. No. But if that's in the 65 ter summary, then it did not come as a surprise perhaps that we heard repetitious evidence in this respect, and that was the issue I raised. If there's anything to be added to it, I'd like to hear it now. Otherwise, we'll adjourn. We will adjourn until ten minutes past six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, my contention is that following a little bit further helpful discussion with Mr. Tieger during the break that the correct and simplest course is I should simply put to the witness the question at page 40, line 25, which was then not answered because we had the -- we had the discussion about the -- what was in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you -- just make sure I've got the context correct. Were you -- Mr. Kecmanovic, were you ever aware of anything that signified that the SDS leadership were not genuinely committed to the Cutileiro Plan if others had supported it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how did you understand what genuine -- "genuinely committed" means exactly; that they would sign or that they would fully implement, or that they would further proceed on the basis of that? What did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is a well-known fact that all three sides signed it. And it's not only the Serb side but the Croat side also did not withdraw their signature. So it was only the Muslim Bosniak side that ultimately did. That is the first point. On this basis, I infer that that is what suited the Croat and the Serb sides. As a matter of fact, now that you're asking me, I think that the Muslim side actually -- Izetbegovic himself, at the moment when he signed the document, he did truly support the plan, but he withdrew it due to other positions apart from his own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that the conversation with Ambassador Zimmermann was already discussed here. That took place between the signature and the withdrawal of the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were the -- were you aware of anything that indicated that the Bosnian Serb leadership did not intend fully to implement the Cutileiro Plan if the Muslims had not withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we go back to Sarajevo, Mr. Kecmanovic? In -- at the time -- let's take the time that you went to Belgrade and then came back to Sarajevo and reported on the agreement that you've reached in Belgrade. How much awareness did you have? How much knowledge did you have of violence in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina over the previous few weeks?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any direct information. I only had indirect information in terms of what was going on outside of Sarajevo. Actually, we already mentioned that there were three cases when I went to the other side. As for going to Belgrade, that was by plane, so I actually flew over the territory outside Sarajevo, so I cannot take that into account as direct contact with the areas outside Sarajevo. As for these other departures from Sarajevo, it was only for an hour or two, for as long as the meetings would take place, and then I'd go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had you yourself heard news of violence in, for example, Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: As for news about what was going on outside Sarajevo, news of course did come in. Newspapers were being printed in Sarajevo, in a reduced form, in all fairness. Newspapers looked like leaflets rather than regular newspapers. And there was also radio information. Very soon there was no electricity in town, so there were transistor radios, and we had the opportunity of listening to radio news, except that -- well, we could listen to the news from both sides, but in both cases, it was war propaganda, and no one could really fully trust what was heard. News were extremely one-sided, so one could only guess about what was actually going on. What I can testify to is actually only the situation in town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say that you could listen to the news from both sides, what was the -- and you're talking about listening, though, you're talking about the radio. What was the -- both sides. What were the actual sources of the news that you're referring to, that you were listening to? I'll make it clear: First of all, what radio stations were you listening to?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, on the one hand it was Radio Sarajevo. That was the city radio. Possibly it was called Radio Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. At any rate, the centre of the broadcast was the town itself. And on the other hand, there were the news from Radio Srna or something like that. I can't remember the name exactly now, but at any rate, that's what same from the Serb side. The Radio of Republika Srpska or something like that, or the Serb Radio. I don't know, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So Radio Sarajevo, what was that? Was that a normal radio station which had been operating for some long time before the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a radio that had been in existence for as long as I can remember. But when the conflict broke out, it was in the service of the war situation. It looked like war propaganda rather than neutral, impartial information that one could trust. And if you would hear something, then you'd know that that is what the situation was like. On the other side, the intonation was more or less the same but of course with a different connotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So far as it was possible for you, Mr. Kecmanovic, to -- to sift out propaganda from something that you felt was reliable, did you in May 1992 have any knowledge of what was going on in - let me take examples - Zvornik, Brcko, Bratunac, Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Well, this is not the media. But once I happened to be in Izetbegovic's office, and his daughter, who was at the same time his secretary and his Chef de Cabinet, entered the room and said to him that he had an urgent call. I know it was from somewhere in Eastern Bosnia. I can't say with certainty that it was Zvornik exactly. And it was something important and did he want to speak to the other party, and he said yes, that he would. And since we were alone in the room, I heard a voice that sounded panic-stricken, excited, upset. And he said that it was a kind of call for help, and he told this man to turn to someone else. However, since this person insisted, I know that Izetbegovic said, "I told you earlier on that a struggle for a state requires sacrifice," and he put the receiver down. And then he told me just in passing that it was somebody from the field that was calling him, from Eastern Bosnia, but I cannot say for sure that it was Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- did you, in May 1992, or before then, of course, did you receive any information about actions of the JNA in other parts of Bosnia? And "other parts" meaning apart from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. No. Nothing that would be out of this pattern that I already described. On the one hand, you had one type of information, and on the other side you had completely opposite information. You could follow both sides and then try to see what the truth was between these two extremes. What I can say, as far as the listeners of the news were concerned, was that among the listeners, among the citizenry there was the same kind of division. Some believed only one source of news, and the others believed only another source of news, which only made tensions go up even further among the citizenry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kecmanovic, you became a member of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency, didn't you, on the 1st of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who were the other members of the Presidency at the point that you joined?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, it was the same Presidency as it was in the beginning, after the elections. The only change was that the late Mr. Nikola Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic were no longer there. Pejanovic and I were there instead of them, and then from the original Presidency Mr. Franjo Boras was no longer there. He was in nominal terms still in the Presidency, but in fact he had been absent for a long time. I think he never went back to the Presidency, although in nominal terms he still had that position because he hadn't resigned. In addition to that Presidency, that is to say Izetbegovic, Abdic, Ganic, Kljuic, there was in view of the fact that a state of war had been declared or, rather, first imminent danger of war, imminent threat of war, something like that, sessions were regularly attended by, but not with the right to vote, Jure Pelivan, who was Prime Minister, and the Chief of General Staff Sefer Halilovic was also present. Also, the vice-president of the Assembly, Mariofil Ljubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The vice-president of the Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik, still being technically the president; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think that Mr. Mariofil Ljubic was treated as a kind of acting president or deputy president in the absence of the president, but at any rate, Mr. Krajisnik was still officially president of parliament. Ljubic, Pelivan and Sefer Halilovic, I think, were just invited to meetings but did not have the status of members all the way up to the declaration of a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was there then -- was there then something that was labelled or known to be called the -- an expanded Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly the presence of the mentioned persons was technically treated as an expanded Presidency, because in fact they were not members and they did not have the right to vote. Basically, they were invited to attend, they could partake in the discussion, but they did not have the right to pass decisions, all the way up to the declaration of the state of war. That is when the situation changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was it clear to those present at the meeting which had a vote and which didn't?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it became clear when decisions were supposed to be reached, and we had to take a vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I think that all of them were not present every time. It depended on the individual case involved. Sometimes it was just one of them or two out of the three. There was no set rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, is this correct -- I'll lead on this, if I may: You imposed -- you and your party imposed three conditions for you to join the Presidency after Koljevic and Plavsic had stepped down. One was that all members of the Presidency should have a right of veto. Two was that all members of the Presidency who were heads of a party should relinquish that position while members of the Presidency, and the third was that the government should be dissolved by the Presidency and replaced by a new government appointed by a new Prime Minister to be appointed by the Presidency. Is that correct? All those were conditions on which you joined the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Working back, the third one, that the government should be dissolved and replaced by a new government appointed by a new Prime Minister, did that happen?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The process had already started. Mr. Pelivan had resigned at the request of the Presidency, and then the procedure was initiated for appointing a new Prime Minister designate. According to the rules of the game, it was supposed to be a Croat, because when top posts were divided up, it was supposed to be a Croat in that position. So it could have been a Croat only. My proposal was Bozidar Matic. He was director general of the biggest and best-known company in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Energoinvest. He was a member of the federal government before the war. Before me he was the dean of the University of Sarajevo, a very prominent figure, very popular. However, Kljuic warned me that even before Pelivan he was offered the Prime Ministership by the Croat side and that he had refused that. Then I asked for approval to talk to him because I thought that he would accept my offer. To cut things short, that's the way it was. However, when I came back with his written acceptance of the Prime Ministership, then the present Croats, especially Kljuic, said that he as a Croat could only come in as a candidate of the HDZ, no one else. In view of the fact that every one of us had the right of veto, that meant that the whole thing was taken off the agenda. The only remaining solution was to extend Pelivan's mandate because the Presidency could no longer continue this bidding for the Prime Ministership.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The second condition, that all members of the Presidency or heads of party should relinquish that position, Mr. Izetbegovic did in fact formally step down as head of the SDA and was replaced by Mr. Mirsad Ceman, is that it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mirsad Ceman was his name; Mirsad Ceman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was he a real head of the SDA, or was he a cypher or something in between?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I knew the man because I was involved in all of those political processes. However, the general public didn't know anything about him. He belonged to a very broad leadership of the SDA. He was not even among the first ten. In other words, he was not the person who was in a position to take the leadership of the party. So this was a mere formality, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just going ahead to the declaration of war that you referred to, when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise answer, although I have a note of that somewhere. In any case, this was in June, during the period while I was in the Presidency. At Izetbegovic's proposal that this should be done, Pejanovic and I had very serious reservations. We announced that we would veto that proposal with the explanation that a declaration of war - in other words a division in the town, a division in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in which a certain percentage of Serbs were represented up to then - would be construed as a war against their fellow nationals and that this would mean a dissolution of the multi-ethnic structure. After that, Izetbegovic took this initiative off the table. That initiative had come from Sefer Halilovic, the Chief of the General Staff. During that night, he called a session without me and Pejanovic, and the explanation was that they couldn't find us on account of the situation of the curfew, of lack of communications, and they held that session during the following night.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As far as you remember, would there have been any difficulty in them finding you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: You know what? Everything was difficult in the town at that time. It was difficult even to come to the regular sessions of the Presidency. It was very difficult to be there every day. And irrespective of that, we came to our workplace every day, and there was a possibility to find us. All the things were not easy. It would not have been easy to find us, but it was doable. Even if there were some special difficulties in finding us, there was no reason for the session not to be held on the following day when we would have certainly been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you became a member of the Presidency, was there -- were there any clear policy guidelines of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. When I entered the Presidency, I was a bit surprised to see that not only there was no written document of the sort but also that there was no initiative to have it done, that nothing was even in the pipeline. That's why I asked for a written listing of the goals of the work of the Presidency under such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you receive such information?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: This was my initiative, to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was something done?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were any steps taken to develop any sort of policy or platform?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: When I established that no such thing existed, I proposed an initiative for a political platform that would govern the work of the Presidency and all the other bodies in the territory of the town, and this would have also spilled over outside of the town. I must admit that some members of the Presidency were delighted to hear my initiative, but there were others, however, who were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were any steps taken, then, to develop such a political platform?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: As a majority of the attendants were interested in my initiative and wanted something like that to be done, a working group was established. The commander of the army; i.e., Chief of the General Staff, showed the biggest support to that initiative. Also, Halilovic said that his soldiers very often asked him what the goals of their struggle was and that a document of that sort would mean a lot to him. Izetbegovic was -- abstained. It was my impression that if there had been such a document, that this would have meant that his hands were tied in his presidential role. Abdic was in favour, and very soon a majority was defined. Nobody was against it. And then a working group was established with Kljuic, Fikret Abdic, and myself in it, and also Pejanovic, and we were tasked with drafting such a document and present it to the Presidency that would then either adopt it immediately or propose amendments to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm lost on a certain matter in which I'd like to find my --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About the declaration of the state of war. Mr. Kecmanovic, you said -- you described the functioning of the Presidency, and you said, "But they did not have the right to pass decisions all the way up to the declaration of the state of war. That is when the situation changed." Then you were further asked about a declaration of war, and you described how there was an initiative by Sefer Halilovic and then that you had reservations just as -- well, you mentioned other names, and finally they -- under Izetbegovic the Presidency, I take it, met during the night when they couldn't find you, and then you said, "He took it off the table." Does that mean that finally the war was never declared, or is that not a correct understanding? Or the state of war was never declared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The way you understood me is correct. There was a declaration of war, however without the support of the Serbian members of the Presidency, since Pejanovic and myself did not attend that particular session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how do I have then to understand your remark that -- I think you said something that "He took it from the table." Let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my fault. I'm not -- I hope I can help on this. I've not completed the question properly. It's entirely my fault. I'd left it dangling. The -- may I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Try and repair what I've done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, there was the meeting at which you and Mr. Pejanovic as well, you had indicated your opposition to there being a declaration of a state of war and at that meeting at which you signified that opposition it was taken off the table. That's right, isn't it? You have to speak into the microphone rather than just nod or ...

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then there was a further meeting, the one at which -- at which they said they couldn't find you, and at that meeting, with you not being there to register your veto, and Mr. Pejanovic not being there to register your veto, the resolution was passed for a declaration of a state of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was entirely my fault, Your Honour. I had left it uncompleted, that particular question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- so you were tasked, the four of you, Kljuic, Abdic, yourself and Pejanovic, you were tasked with drafting the document, presenting it to the Presidency. Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did that. As a matter of fact, the document in question was drafted by me, and then Pejanovic and Abdic and also Kljuic elaborated this draft that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How long did it take to produce, roughly?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Not long, because I had already had a draft of such a document in another document. There was a party document that the Alliance of Reformists had prepared in the meantime. Let me -- let me -- let me explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it produced within two weeks?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the most. Maybe even within ten days. If I may explain. If I may clarify. When the situation changed and when the war started, my party was fortunate or unfortunate, if you will, to somehow adjust its strategy, programme and policies to the newly arisen situation. Of course we did not have time for some grand meetings, but we had to respect the democratic procedure and the inner leadership drafted a document that served as a basis for the platform as my view how things should look like, and this is what I gave to Pejanovic for further elaboration. And in a certain way they just fine tuned this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what, if you can say, were the essential features of the proposals in the document?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: What was original about this document, together with some generally accepted and acceptable principles, were some elements from Cutileiro's plan that were incorporated into that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the elements from the Cutileiro Plan that were incorporated were what?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In a nutshell, I can tell you that we started from the fact that it was necessary to carry out some sort of decentralisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that some territorial ethnic units should be established with political autonomy or, rather, ethnic autonomy and political self-government. The focus of that was the fact that we had to start not from the newly arisen situation that was caused by war and force but, rather, that we should start from the situation as it was then. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is a tradition and history of territorial and ethnic division. There were regions that had its territorial and ethnic specificities. For example, Western Herzegovina. In the period before the war, during the communism and even before that, Western Herzegovina was not just a geographical term. When somebody said Western Herzegovina, everybody knew that it was a predominantly Croatian region. When somebody mentioned Cazinska Krajina, where is a region where Fikret Abdic hailed from, alternatively we called it the Green Krajina, and everybody in Bosnia-Herzegovina knew that this was predominantly Muslim territory. If somebody mentioned Central Bosnia, of -- it was a well-known fact that this was dominated by Muslims, but that in Bosnian Krajina there is a predominantly Serb population. And we believed that this is the good basis on which we could execute that decentralisation in order to create regions or cantons. At that time there was no mention of entities. This came only after the Dayton. It was the cantons. And this was a similarity with Cutileiro's plan. We also established that the large urban centres or zones of mixed population, particularly in big towns, and that those towns should remain extra-territorial, and in that I mean Sarajevo and some other bigger urban centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours. Excuse me, Mr. Kecmanovic. Your Honours, about three minutes to go. I have a point which I do need to raise this evening in the absence of the witness, and in fact in closed session, Your Honour, about the way in which we should proceed first thing tomorrow morning. May I do that now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Kecmanovic, we'll stop for the day as far as you're concerned. We have to continue for a couple of minutes. I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak to anyone about the testimony you have given until now or you're still about to give tomorrow and perhaps Wednesday. You should not speak with anyone about it. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom. Then would you please follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before we go into private session, there is one point I would wish to raise and maybe it's more convenient --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think under the normal course of business we would remain in open session for this. Simply this Your Honour: Again with respect to the 65 ter summary, there are several matters that were elicited during the course of this witness's testimony that are not covered in the 65 ter. I am not anticipating at this point that it's going to cause a delay in the proceedings, although I need to look at that, but I do note that Mr. Stewart would seem to be working off of a multi-page document from -- in short, that those areas weren't elicited inadvertently and unexpectedly, and I would ask again that, to the extent possible, the Prosecution be advised as -- well, within the Rules and -- but at least as far as in advance as possible, if we can't meet the 14-day deadline, what the facts that are intended to be elicited from the witness will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do my best. I'm working from a multi-page document last saved at about half past one today, so there are simply limits, I'm afraid, to -- we do our best, Your Honour, but there are limits to how much a document in those circumstances can then be transmitted in 65 ter form. It's as simple and as practical as that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if I look at the 65 ter summary, under 4, for example, I see mainly one meeting, if I'm correct, where the witness testified about three meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not disputing the general point. We -- we hardly ever do, actually, neither Mr. Josse nor I, dispute the unsatisfactory position in relation to 65 ters, and I don't here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to add something, especially to the first meeting. Well, you spent not much but at least five minutes on that first meeting, which learned us that they went there by taxi, that no specific issues were really discussed apart from some concerns expressed, that at the end of the meeting they understood that Serbs understood each other better than peoples of different ethnicities, and the one point which might have some relevance sufficient enough, I would say, to raise the issue is that if you invite the SDS leadership that -- and not being very specific, expecting either Mr. Koljevic or anyone else, that Mr. Krajisnik turns up, but apart from that, the whole of the meeting from what I perceived until now could have left out without -- but again what I at this moment consider to be the Defence case -- without too much damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour appreciates I don't ask the witness how he travels to the meeting. If he tells the Trial Chamber he travels by taxi, he tells us he travels by taxi. I don't want to know that and I don't want the Trial Chamber to know it, but I can't help it if the witness tells me. But Your Honour, I accept the basic point but Your Honour, in relation to these meetings -- well, Your Honour, I have to go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in private session, yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of April, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
